transfers.text: UA p. 13 Table II lists the Fighter for any armor, shield, and weapons; oil is permitted and poison is the DM’s option. UA p. 26 lists four initial weapon proficiencies, a −2 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per three levels.

UA p. 18 allows weapon specialization only for Fighters and Rangers, chosen at character creation and costing two weapon-proficiency slots. From the initial allotment of four Fighter or three Ranger weapons, ordinary specialization leaves one specialist weapon plus two or one other proficient weapons; bow specialization (but not crossbow specialization) costs one extra slot, leaving the Fighter one other proficiency and the Ranger none. A melee specialist gains +1 to hit and +2 damage. A bow specialist has 6–30-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage on a successful hit) and +1 to hit and damage at short range; the bow can be fired before initiative if the arrow is nocked, shaft drawn, and target in sight. A crossbow specialist has 6–60-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage), short range +1 to hit and damage, and medium range +1 to hit only; it can fire before initiative if cocked, aimed, and the target is in range. Other missile specialists gain +1 to hit and +2 damage. Specialization hit bonuses are not magical and do not enable hits on creatures affected only by magical weapons. Use the existing UA specialization-rate table for weapon-specific rates; it supersedes ordinary rates while the specialist weapon is used.

UA p. 18 distinguishes the initial specialization choice, made when the character is created, from double specialization, which a fighter or ranger may choose initially or later for the same specific weapon type already specialized in. Double specialization is limited to melee weapons other than pole arms and the two-handed sword; it uses the proficiency slot that would otherwise gain a new weapon and grants +3 to hit and +3 damage. For ordinary melee specialization, +1 to hit and +2 damage stack with Strength and magic bonuses, and the weapon must be a specific type (for example, long sword rather than “sword”). For a crossbow specialist, the 6–60-foot point-blank category completely replaces a light crossbow’s ordinary short range in a dungeon.

UA pp. 21–22 add situation-specific tracking procedures to the Ranger’s level-by-level base chances already recorded in this class entry. Outdoors, the base is 10% per level plus 10%, with a 110% base ceiling; terrain, group size, crossing/overtracking, trail age, precipitation, and deliberate concealment modify the attempt. Indoor tracking uses separate surface categories, the same base and specified shared modifiers, and additional observation prerequisites; movement rate depends on track clarity and illumination. Apply the printed definitions and impossibility limits, and keep the p. 22 identification roll separate from the tracking roll.
UA p. 21 distinguishes the outdoor base-chance ceiling of 110% from the final adjusted chance: after modifiers, an adjusted chance above 100% is treated as 100%.

UA p. 13 Table II lists the cavalier for any armor, shield, and weapons, subject to note 1’s social-station limits on armor and arms; note 2 bars oil in personal combat but permits siege use, and poison is listed only if evil. Use the six social-station packages on p. 25; each horse is supplied with station-appropriate tack, harness, saddle, and saddlebags, and a cavalier below Upper Class begins as a 0-level Horseman to be taken in by a good family and esquired.

UA p. 26 lists the cavalier weapon-proficiency row as 3*, a −3 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per two levels. Its star note specifies 0-level Horseman/Lancer and 1st-level Armiger counts and restricts Cavalier weapon choices.
UA p. 13 Table II permits any armor, shield, and weapons, but note 3 limits the class Dexterity armor benefit in bulky or fairly bulky armor.

UA p. 18 requires the barbarian’s initial weapon proficiencies to include hand axe, knife, and spear; other weapons based on the native area may be chosen by the DM. The p. 26 weapon table lists six initial proficiencies, a −1 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per two levels; these weapon slots are separate from the barbarian’s nonweapon abilities.

UA pp. 19–20 group barbarian abilities as eight primary abilities (climbing, hiding, surprise, back protection, leaping/springing, detecting illusion, detecting magic, leadership), four secondary abilities (survival, first aid, outdoor craft, tracking), and one or more locale- or culture-selected tertiary skills. All four secondary abilities are possessed, but are generally limited in unfamiliar areas until about a month of continuous exposure; the DM determines applicable tertiary skills. Paddled and rowed small craft are separate tertiary options.

UA p. 20 names eight locale- or culture-selected tertiary skill options: animal handling, horsemanship, long-distance signalling, running, small craft (paddled), small craft (rowed), sound imitation, and snare building. The DM determines which apply to the campaign; a barbarian has one or more.

UA p. 13 Table II lists the Acrobat’s armor as “as thief,” no shield, and weapons “as thief, plus lasso and staff”; oil is permitted and poison is the DM’s option. Note 4 directs armor other than leather to the function adjustments in Thieves Table II (p. 22).

UA p. 25 Tables II and III adjust the Acrobat’s base function chances or maxima for Strength and Dexterity; apply their stated racial adjustments as well. Table IV separates body-associated weight (clothing, accessories, armor, weapons) from additional carried weight, which applies only while tightrope walking; backpacks are otherwise barred during Acrobat activities. Its level-14 extra 1,000 gp and level-22 passenger examples are limited by the accompanying procedure.
UA p. 26 lists the Acrobat weapon-proficiency row as 2 initial weapons, a −3 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per four levels.
UA p. 13 Table II lists any armor, shield, and weapons subject to note 1’s social-station limits; note 2 bars oil in personal combat but permits siege use, and poison is never permitted.

UA p. 26 shows a starred Paladin weapon-proficiency entry (3*, −3, one added proficiency per two levels). The star note defines zero-level Cavalier grades and names Cavalier/Ranger weapon-choice restrictions, but does not explain the Paladin star; keep that meaning unresolved.

UA p. 13 Table II restricts the Druid to leather or padded armor, a wooden shield, and the listed weapons (aklys, club, dagger, dart, garrot, hammer, lasso, sap, sling, scimitar, spear, staff, staff sling, sword (khopesh), and whip); oil is permitted and poison is the DM’s option.
UA p. 26 lists the Druid weapon-proficiency row as 2 initial weapons, a −4 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per five levels.
